- **withdraw** — withdrew — withdrawn

### B.4 Семьи с чередованием гласного и какие пятьдесят глаголов выучить первыми

Ряд глаголов группы A-B-C из B.3 — не случайный полтинник исключений: несколько из них образуют небольшие семейства, все меняющие гласный одинаковым образом, — окаменелость гораздо более регулярной системы, которая некогда была в древнеанглийском (система «сильных глаголов»). Распознавание семейства облегчает удержание форм в памяти, потому что вы учите один рисунок вместо нескольких не связанных друг с другом слов.

Самое чёткое семейство идёт по схеме **i → a → u**: *sing — sang — sung*, *ring — rang — rung*, *drink — drank — drunk*, *sink — sank — sunk*, *shrink — shrank — shrunk*, *stink — stank — stunk*, *spring — sprang — sprung*, *swim — swam — swum*, и, с небольшим отличием в написании, *begin — began — begun*. Если вам встречается новый неправильный глагол, у которого в базовой форме краткий звук **i** стоит перед носовым согласным или перед *-ing*, это первый рисунок, который стоит попробовать.

Второе семейство идёт по схеме **база на -ow или -y → -ew → -own**: *blow — blew — blown*, *grow — grew — grown*, *know — knew — known*, *throw — threw — thrown* и *fly — flew — flown* (исключение, поскольку его база не оканчивается на *-ow*, но форма прошедшего времени и причастие следуют той же схеме).

Третье, более рыхлое семейство сужает гласный базовой формы до *o* в прошедшем времени и добавляет *-en* для причастия: *speak — spoke — spoken*, *break — broke — broken*, *wake — woke — woken*, *steal — stole — stolen*, *freeze — froze — frozen*, *choose — chose — chosen*. Не пытайтесь втиснуть каждый новый глагол в одно из этих трёх семейств — немало глаголов группы B.3 (*go — went — gone*, *be — was/were — been*, *do — did — done*) неправильны даже по меркам этого списка, — но сначала проверьте семейство: это избавит вас от заучивания каждого глагола с чистого листа.

Если вы изучаете это приложение впервые, не начинайте с *arise* и не идите дальше по алфавиту. Начните с полусотни глаголов, несущих основную нагрузку в обычной речи и письме, — каждый из них уже есть в B.1–B.3 выше; вот лишь порядок, в котором их стоит учить:

**be, have, do, say, get, make, go, know, take, see, come, think, give, find, tell, become, show, leave, feel, put, bring, begin, keep, hold, write, stand, hear, let, mean, set, meet, run, pay, sit, speak, lead, understand, win, teach, sell, send, build, break, spend, grow, buy, wear, choose, drive, fall.**

Как только эти пятьдесят становятся автоматическими, остальные глаголы приложения заметно ниже по частотности, и их можно усваивать по мере встречи в чтении.

### B.5 Совпадают основа и простое прошедшее (A-A-B)

Небольшая группа, в которой базовая форма и форма прошедшего времени совпадают, а причастие прошедшего времени — другое. Ловушка — именно причастие: поскольку форма прошедшего времени выглядит в точности как базовая, изучающие предполагают, что и причастие такое же, и производят ✗ *I have beat him* вместо ✓ *I have beaten him*.

- **beat** — beat — beaten

### B.6 Совпадают основа и причастие прошедшего времени (A-B-A)

Зеркальный случай: базовая форма и причастие прошедшего времени совпадают, и различается только форма прошедшего времени. Именно этот рисунок стоит за двумя самыми заметными на слух ошибками английского языка — ✗ *I have ran* и ✗ *I have came*, — поскольку форма прошедшего времени — это форма, за которой изучающие тянутся в первую очередь.

- **become** — became — become
- **come** — came — come
- **run** — ran — run
- **overcome** — overcame — overcome
- **outrun** — outran — outrun

Обратите внимание, что демонстрируют вместе B.5 и B.6: три группы выше не исчерпывают всех возможностей. Неправильные глаголы английского языка образуют пять моделей, а не три, — и две самые маленькие группы содержат одни из самых высокочастотных глаголов языка, что как раз и объясняет, почему ошибки в них так заметны.

---

lessons.title: Appendix C. 200+ Common Phrasal Verbs
lessons.titleRu: Appendix C. Более 200 распространённых фразовых глаголов
lessons.grammarMd:
A phrasal verb is a verb plus one or two particles (*look up*, *put up with*) whose meaning is often not predictable from the parts — to *look up* a word has nothing to do with looking or being up. This is ordinary spoken and written English, not slang: native speakers use phrasal verbs constantly, and their single-word synonyms (*investigate* for *look into*, *tolerate* for *put up with*) usually sound more formal or more written. Avoiding phrasal verbs doesn't make your English more correct — it makes it sound like a translation.

How it's organised: the list groups entries under the base verb they're built from, because that is how they are easiest to learn. Once you know how many particles *get* combines with, you are learning one verb's range rather than a dozen unrelated items. Twenty-two base verbs — the ones that generate most of the phrasal verbs in ordinary English — have a section each:

*be, break, bring, call, carry, come, cut, do, drop, fall, get, give, go, hand, hold, keep, let, look, make, put, take, turn.*

They appear in this order: *look* (C.1), *get* (C.2), *take* (C.3), *put* (C.4), *make* (C.5), then the remaining seventeen alphabetically (C.7–C.23). The final section, **C.6 Others**, collects common phrasal verbs built on base verbs that generate only a handful each — *draw, find, hang, mix, pass, pick, pull, run, see, set, show, sort, stand, stay, stick, wake, watch, wear, work, write* — listed alphabetically. (The numbering runs out of sequence because section numbers, once published, are fixed; read it as C.1–C.5, C.7–C.23, then C.6.)

A note on the *be* group (C.7): *be up to*, *be over*, *be off* and their relatives are not phrasal verbs in the narrowest technical sense — the particle usually keeps a recognisable meaning of its own. They are included because they behave like the rest in practice: idiomatic, unpredictable from the parts, and constant in speech.

Several particles carry a recognisable core meaning across many different base verbs, even though each combination still has to be learned individually. **Out** very often adds a sense of emergence, removal, or exhaustion: information *comes out* or is *found out*, students *drop out*, a supply *runs out*. **Off** very often adds separation or disconnection: you *take off* a coat, *get off* a bus, *turn off* a light, a handle *comes off*, a plan is *called off*. **Up** is the least consistent of the three: sometimes it adds completion or intensification (*draw up* a contract, *break up* a relationship for good, *hang up* a call), but just as often it simply signals upward movement or arrival (*get up*, *show up*, *turn up*) with no sense of "finishing" involved at all. Treat these three patterns as a helpful first guess when you meet a new phrasal verb, never as a rule — the gloss given for each entry below is the one to trust.

Which entries to learn first: prioritise the ones that come up in ordinary conversation about daily plans, not the more literary ones. From the lists below, learn these before the rest: *look after, look for, look forward to, get up, get on, get off, get back, get away, take off, take away, put on, put off, put up with, make up, make up for, come back, come on, come in, come out, go on, go out, find out, turn on, turn off, turn out, turn up, bring up, break down, break up, hold on, hang on, hang out, set up, sort out, show up, run out, pick up, work out, wake up*. Everything else in this appendix is genuinely useful but lower-frequency; come back for it once the list above is automatic.

Each entry below now carries a short example sentence in addition to its meaning gloss, so you can see the phrasal verb working in context rather than as an isolated definition.

### C.1 With *look*
- **look after** — take care of — *Can you look after my cat this weekend?*
- **look at** — examine — *Let me look at that cut on your hand.*
- **look back** — reminisce — *She likes to look back on her school days.*
- **look down on** — despise — *He looks down on people who never went to university.*
- **look for** — seek — *I'm looking for my keys.*
- **look forward to** — anticipate eagerly (+ ing) — *We're looking forward to seeing you.*
- **look into** — investigate — *The police are looking into the complaint.*
- **look on** — observe without acting — *The crowd just looked on as the argument continued.*
- **look out** — be careful — *Look out! There's a car coming.*
- **look out for** — watch for — *Look out for the blue sign on the left.*
- **look over** — review — *Could you look over my essay before I submit it?*
- **look through** — scan — *She looked through the report quickly before the meeting.*
- **look up** — search (information) — *If you don't know the word, look it up.*
- **look up to** — admire — *Younger players really look up to him.*

### C.2 With *get*
- **get across** — communicate — *He struggled to get his point across.*
- **get along with** — have good relations — *She gets along with everyone in the office.*
- **get around** — avoid; move about — *He found a way to get around the rule.*
- **get at** — imply; reach — *What exactly are you trying to get at?*
- **get away** — escape — *The thief got away before the police arrived.*
- **get away with** — avoid punishment — *He lied and somehow got away with it.*
- **get back** — return — *We got back from holiday on Sunday.*
- **get by** — survive barely — *They get by on a small pension.*
- **get down** — descend; depress — *All this bad news is getting me down.*
- **get down to** — start seriously — *Let's get down to business.*
- **get in** — enter — *What time does the train get in?*
- **get into** — enter; become involved — *She got into an argument with her neighbour.*
- **get off** — alight; leave work — *I get off work at six today.*
- **get on** — board; progress — *How are you getting on with the new job?*
- **get out** — leave — *Get out of the rain.*
- **get out of** — avoid; escape — *He got out of doing the dishes again.*
- **get over** — recover from — *It took her weeks to get over the flu.*
- **get through** — complete; reach by phone — *I finally got through to the helpline.*
- **get to** — arrive at — *What time will we get to the airport?*
- **get together** — meet — *Let's get together for lunch next week.*
- **get up** — rise from bed — *I get up at six every morning.*
- **get used to** — accustom to (+ ing) — *You'll get used to the noise eventually.*

### C.3 With *take*
- **take after** — resemble — *She takes after her mother.*
- **take apart** — disassemble — *He took the engine apart to clean it.*
- **take away** — remove — *They took away his driving licence.*
- **take back** — return; retract — *I take back what I said earlier.*
- **take down** — write; disassemble — *Can you take down these notes for me?*
- **take in** — understand; deceive; shelter — *The lecture was so fast I couldn't take it all in.*
- **take off** — remove; depart — *The plane took off an hour late.*
- **take on** — undertake; hire — *The firm is taking on ten new staff.*
- **take out** — remove; go out with (date) — *He took her out for dinner.*
- **take over** — assume control — *The new manager takes over next month.*
- **take to** — start liking — *The children took to their new teacher immediately.*
- **take up** — begin hobby; occupy — *She took up painting last year.*

### C.4 With *put*
- **put away** — store — *Put your toys away before dinner.*
- **put down** — insult; place; kill (animal) — *He gently put down the sleeping baby.*
- **put forward** — suggest — *She put forward a new proposal at the meeting.*
- **put in** — install; spend (time) — *They put in a new kitchen last year.*
- **put off** — postpone; deter — *Let's not put off the decision any longer.*
- **put on** — wear; gain (weight) — *Put on your coat, it's cold outside.*
- **put out** — extinguish; inconvenience — *Firefighters put out the blaze within an hour.*
- **put through** — connect (phone); cause to endure — *Could you put me through to sales, please?*
- **put up** — erect; accommodate — *They put up a tent by the river.*
- **put up with** — tolerate — *I can't put up with this noise any longer.*

### C.5 With *make*
- **make out** — understand; kiss passionately — *I could barely make out what she was saying.*
- **make over** — redo — *They made over the old barn into a guesthouse.*
- **make up** — invent; reconcile; apply cosmetics — *He made up an excuse for being late.*
- **make up for** — compensate — *Nothing can make up for the time we lost.*
- **make for** — head toward; contribute to — *We made for the nearest exit.* / *Long meetings make for short tempers.*
- **make of** — interpret, form an opinion about — *I don't know what to make of her reply.*
- **make off with** — steal and escape — *Someone made off with my umbrella.*
- **make out of** — construct from — *The sculpture was made out of scrap metal.*
- **make do (with)** — manage with what is available — *There's no cream, so we'll have to make do with milk.*
- **make it** — arrive; succeed; survive — *Sorry, I can't make it on Friday.*
- **make up to** — try to get into someone's favour (informal) — *He's been making up to the new manager all week.*

### C.7 With *be*

*Be* plus a particle is not a phrasal verb in the strictest sense — the particle usually keeps a recognisable meaning, and many of these sit on the border with ordinary prepositional phrases. They are grouped here because they behave like the others in use: they are idiomatic, they are extremely frequent in speech, and the single-word equivalents (*attend*, *conclude*, *support*) all sound more formal.

- **be after** — be pursuing, be trying to get — *I think he's after my job.*
- **be away** — be absent, be travelling — *She's away on business until Thursday.*
- **be back** — have returned — *I'll be back in ten minutes.*
- **be down** — not be working (of systems); be depressed — *The whole network is down again.*
- **be for** — support — *Are you for or against the proposal?*
- **be in** — be at home or in the office — *Is Dr Adams in this afternoon?*
- **be into** — be keenly interested in (informal) — *He's really into cycling at the moment.*
- **be off** — leave; be cancelled; be spoiled (of food) — *Right, I'm off — see you tomorrow.* / *The wedding's off.* / *This milk is off.*
- **be on** — be taking place; be showing — *What's on at the cinema tonight?*
- **be out** — be absent; be published; be extinguished — *Her new book is out next month.*
- **be over** — be finished — *The meeting was over by four.*
- **be through (with)** — have finished (with) — *I'm through with excuses.*
- **be up** — be awake and out of bed; be wrong (informal) — *He's been up since five.* / *Something's up — she hasn't answered all day.*
- **be up to** — be doing (often something suspect); be capable of; be the responsibility of — *What have you been up to?* / *He isn't up to the job.* / *It's up to you.*

### C.8 With *break*

- **break away** — separate from a group — *Three regions broke away from the federation.*
- **break down** — stop functioning; weep; analyse into parts — *My car broke down on the motorway.*
- **break in** — enter forcefully; interrupt — *Burglars broke in through the back window.*
- **break into** — enter by force; suddenly start (laughing, running) — *She broke into a run when she saw the bus.*
- **break off** — detach; end (relationship or talks) — *They broke off their engagement last month.*
- **break out** — escape; erupt (war, fire, disease) — *A fire broke out in the warehouse.*
- **break out in** — become covered in (a rash, sweat) — *He broke out in a rash after eating shellfish.*
- **break through** — force a way past an obstacle — *Researchers finally broke through after years of failure.*
- **break up** — end (relationship); separate; begin school holidays (**UK**) — *They broke up after five years together.*

### C.9 With *bring*

- **bring about** — cause — *The reforms brought about real change.*
- **bring along** — take with you — *Bring your brother along if he's free.*
- **bring around / round** — persuade; revive from unconsciousness — *It took an hour to bring him round to our view.*
- **bring back** — revive (a memory); return; reintroduce — *That song brings back memories.*
- **bring down** — lower; defeat; topple — *The scandal brought down the government.*
- **bring forward** — move to an earlier time; propose — *The meeting has been brought forward to Monday.*
- **bring in** — introduce; earn — *The new law brings in stricter penalties.*
- **bring off** — succeed at something difficult — *Nobody thought they'd bring it off.*
- **bring on** — cause (something unwelcome) — *The stress brought on a migraine.*
- **bring out** — release; reveal a quality — *The company is bringing out a new model next year.*
- **bring up** — raise (a child); mention — *She was brought up by her grandparents.*

### C.10 With *call*

- **call back** — return a call; visit again — *I'll call you back in ten minutes.*
- **call by** — visit briefly (**UK**) — *I'll call by on my way home.*
- **call for** — require; collect someone — *This situation calls for immediate action.*
- **call in** — summon; drop in briefly — *They called in a specialist to fix the problem.*
- **call off** — cancel — *The match was called off because of rain.*
- **call on** — visit briefly; appeal to someone to act — *We called on an old friend on the way home.*
- **call out** — shout; summon (emergency services); publicly criticise — *She called out his name across the street.*
- **call round** — visit (**UK**) — *Call round any time this weekend.*
- **call up** — telephone; conscript — *He called up his brother to share the news.*

### C.11 With *carry*

- **carry off** — succeed at something difficult; win — *It was an awkward speech, but she carried it off.*
- **carry on** — continue; have an affair (informal) — *Carry on, I'm listening.*
- **carry out** — perform, execute (an order, a plan, research) — *The team carried out a full inspection.*
- **carry over** — transfer to a later period — *Unused leave can be carried over to next year.*
- **carry through** — complete despite difficulty; sustain someone — *Her determination carried her through the worst months.*
- **be carried away** — get over-excited and lose judgement — *Sorry, I got carried away and bought three of them.*

*Carry out* is the highest-value entry in this group: it is the ordinary, neutral verb for performing an instruction, an experiment or a piece of work, and it appears constantly in written and workplace English.

### C.12 With *come*

- **come about** — happen — *How did this misunderstanding come about?*
- **come across** — find by chance — *I came across an old photo in the attic.*
- **come across as** — give an impression of being — *He comes across as rather shy.*
- **come along** — progress; accompany — *The project is coming along nicely.*
- **come apart** — fall to pieces — *The old book came apart in my hands.*
- **come around / round** — regain consciousness; change your mind; visit — *She eventually came round to the idea.*
- **come back** — return — *She came back from Paris yesterday.*
- **come between** — damage a relationship — *Don't let money come between you.*
- **come down** — descend; fall (of prices) — *Prices have come down a lot this year.*
- **come down to** — be essentially a matter of — *It all comes down to money in the end.*
- **come down with** — catch an illness — *He's come down with a cold.*
- **come in** — enter; finish (in a race) — *Please, come in and sit down.*
- **come into** — inherit — *She came into a small fortune last year.*
- **come off** — detach; happen successfully — *The handle came off the door.*
- **come on** — start; hurry up; improve — *Come on, we're going to be late!*
- **come out** — emerge; be published; reveal one's orientation — *The truth finally came out during the trial.*
- **come over** — visit; be overcome by a feeling — *Why don't you come over for dinner tonight?*
- **come through** — succeed; survive — *He came through the surgery without complications.*
- **come up** — arise — *Something urgent has come up at work.*
- **come up against** — encounter (a difficulty) — *We came up against a lot of resistance.*
- **come up with** — devise — *She came up with a clever solution.*

### C.13 With *cut*

- **cut across** — take a shortcut through; transcend (categories) — *The issue cuts across party lines.*
- **cut back (on)** — reduce — *We're cutting back on advertising this year.*
- **cut down (on)** — reduce consumption; fell (a tree) — *He's trying to cut down on sugar.*
- **cut in** — interrupt; pull in front of a vehicle — *She kept cutting in while I was talking.*
- **cut off** — disconnect; isolate; interrupt — *We were cut off in the middle of the call.*
- **cut out** — remove; stop doing (informal); stall (of an engine) — *Cut out the noise, please.*
- **cut short** — end earlier than planned — *They cut the holiday short when he fell ill.*
- **cut up** — divide into pieces — *Cut the vegetables up before you add them.*

Note the near-synonyms *cut back on* and *cut down on*: both mean "reduce", and both are correct in most contexts. *Cut down on* dominates for personal habits (*cut down on coffee*); *cut back on* dominates for budgets and organisations (*cut back on spending*).

### C.14 With *do*

- **do away with** — abolish — *The new policy did away with the old dress code.*
- **do in** — exhaust (informal); kill (slang) — *That walk has completely done me in.*
- **do out of** — cheat someone of something — *He was done out of his share of the profits.*
- **do over** — repeat (**US**) — *The essay was so bad he had to do it over.*
- **do up** — fasten; renovate — *Do up your jacket, it's freezing.*
- **do with** — benefit from (in *could do with*) — *I could do with a coffee.*
- **do without** — manage without — *We'll have to do without a car for a while.*

### C.15 With *drop*

- **drop back** — fall behind deliberately — *He dropped back to run with the slower group.*
- **drop by** — visit briefly — *Feel free to drop by any time.*
- **drop in** — visit unexpectedly — *An old friend dropped in yesterday afternoon.*
- **drop off** — decrease; deliver; fall asleep — *I'll drop off the kids at school first.*
- **drop out** — quit (school, a race) — *He dropped out of university after a year.*

### C.16 With *fall*

- **fall apart** — disintegrate; break down emotionally — *The old shed is falling apart.*
- **fall back on** — resort to as a reserve — *If the deal fails, we can fall back on the old supplier.*
- **fall behind** — lag — *She fell behind with her rent payments.*
- **fall for** — be deceived by; fall in love with — *He fell for her the moment they met.*
- **fall off** — decrease — *Sales have fallen off since the summer.*
- **fall out** — quarrel — *The two brothers fell out over money.*
- **fall through** — fail to happen — *Our holiday plans fell through at the last minute.*

### C.17 With *give*

- **give away** — donate; reveal (a secret); hand over a bride — *Don't give away the ending.*
- **give back** — return — *Give me back my pen, please.*
- **give in** — surrender, stop resisting; hand in (**UK**) — *He argued for an hour before giving in.*
- **give off** — emit (a smell, heat, light) — *The lamp gives off a lot of heat.*
- **give out** — distribute; run out; stop working — *Her patience finally gave out.*
- **give over** — stop it (informal, **UK**) — *Oh, give over — you don't believe that.*
- **give up** — quit; stop trying; surrender — *She gave up smoking two years ago.*
- **give up on** — stop believing in or hoping for — *Don't give up on him yet.*
- **give way (to)** — collapse; yield priority — *The old bridge gave way under the weight.*

*Give up* deserves special attention because it is separable and carries an object in two positions: *give up smoking* / *give it up* — never ✗ *give up it*. Pronoun objects always go in the middle (Chapter 149).

### C.18 With *go*

- **go after** — pursue — *The company is going after new markets abroad.*
- **go against** — oppose — *Their decision goes against company policy.*
- **go ahead** — proceed — *You can go ahead and start without me.*
- **go along with** — agree to — *I'll go along with whatever you decide.*
- **go away** — leave; depart on holiday — *We're going away for a few days.*
- **go back** — return — *We need to go back and check the numbers.*
- **go by** — elapse; judge by — *Don't go by first impressions alone.*
- **go down** — decrease; sink; be received (well/badly) — *The ship went down in a storm.*
- **go down with** — become ill with (**UK**) — *Half the office has gone down with flu.*
- **go for** — like; attempt; attack — *I think I'll go for the salad today.*
- **go in for** — participate in; be keen on — *She's never really gone in for sports.*
- **go into** — enter (a profession); examine in detail — *I won't go into the details now.*
- **go off** — explode; sound (of an alarm); spoil (of food); stop liking (**UK**) — *The alarm went off at midnight.*
- **go on** — continue; happen — *Please, go on with your story.*
- **go out** — exit; date; be extinguished — *They've been going out for two years.*
- **go over** — review — *Let's go over the figures once more.*
- **go round** — be enough for everyone (**UK**); visit — *There aren't enough chairs to go round.*
- **go through** — endure; examine; be approved — *She's been through a lot this year.*
- **go through with** — carry out despite doubts — *In the end he couldn't go through with it.*
- **go under** — sink; fail (of a business) — *Many small shops went under during the recession.*
- **go up** — rise — *House prices have gone up sharply.*
- **go with** — match; accompany — *That scarf goes well with your coat.*
- **go without** — manage without — *They went without heating all winter.*

### C.19 With *hand*

- **hand back** — return — *He handed back the keys without a word.*
- **hand down** — pass to the next generation; deliver (a verdict) — *The recipe was handed down from her grandmother.*
- **hand in** — submit — *Please hand in your assignments by Friday.*
- **hand on** — pass to the next person — *Read it and hand it on.*
- **hand out** — distribute — *The teacher handed out the test papers.*
- **hand over** — surrender; transfer responsibility — *The suspect handed over the stolen goods.*
- **hand round** — pass around a group (**UK**) — *She handed round a plate of biscuits.*

### C.20 With *hold*

- **hold back** — restrain; withhold information — *He held back his anger during the meeting.*
- **hold down** — keep (a job); restrain — *He's never held down a job for more than a year.*
- **hold off** — delay; keep at a distance — *Let's hold off on a decision until Friday.*
- **hold on** — wait; endure; grip — *Hold on, let me check the schedule.*
- **hold onto** — keep, not give away — *Hold onto that receipt.*
- **hold out** — offer; last; resist — *Our supplies won't hold out much longer.*
- **hold up** — delay; rob; remain valid — *The traffic held us up for an hour.*

### C.21 With *keep*

- **keep away (from)** — avoid — *Keep away from the edge.*
- **keep back** — withhold; stay at a distance — *He kept back the most important detail.*
- **keep down** — restrain; retain (food) — *Try to keep the noise down after ten.*
- **keep from** — prevent; refrain from — *Nothing could keep her from finishing.*
- **keep off** — stay away from; avoid (a topic, a food) — *Keep off the grass.*
- **keep on** — continue — *He kept on talking even after the bell rang.*
- **keep out** — stay outside; exclude — *Keep out — construction area.*
- **keep to** — adhere to; stay on — *Please keep to the schedule.*
- **keep up** — maintain — *It's hard to keep up this pace all day.*
- **keep up with** — keep pace with; stay informed about — *She struggles to keep up with the coursework.*

### C.22 With *let*

- **let down** — disappoint; lower; lengthen (clothing) — *He felt he had let his team down.*
- **let in** — admit — *Could you let the cat in, please?*
- **let in for** — involve someone in trouble — *I didn't know what I was letting myself in for.*
- **let off** — excuse; discharge (a weapon, a firework) — *The teacher let him off with a warning.*
- **let on** — reveal a secret — *Don't let on that we know.*
- **let out** — release; enlarge (clothing); emit (a sound) — *They let the prisoners out early for good behaviour.*
- **let up** — become less intense — *The rain finally let up around noon.*

### C.23 With *turn*

- **turn against** — become hostile to — *The public soon turned against the policy.*
- **turn around / round** — reverse; recover — *The company managed to turn around its finances.*
- **turn away** — refuse entry to — *Dozens of fans were turned away at the door.*
- **turn back** — reverse a journey — *The weather forced them to turn back.*
- **turn down** — reject; reduce (volume, heat) — *He turned down the job offer.*
- **turn in** — submit; retire for the night — *I'm exhausted, I think I'll turn in early.*
- **turn into** — become — *The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.*
- **turn off** — deactivate; leave a road; repel (informal) — *Don't forget to turn off the lights.*
- **turn on** — activate; attack suddenly — *Can you turn on the heating?*
- **turn out** — prove to be; attend; produce; extinguish — *The party turned out better than expected.*
- **turn over** — flip; hand to the authorities; have a turnover of — *He turned over the papers to the police.*
- **turn to** — seek help from; switch to — *She had no one to turn to.*
- **turn up** — appear; increase (volume) — *She turned up an hour late.*

### C.6 Others

Base verbs that produce only a few common phrasal verbs each, listed alphabetically. Everything built on the twenty-two high-frequency base verbs is in C.1–C.5 and C.7–C.23 above.

- **draw up** — compose; stop (vehicle) — *The lawyer drew up a new contract.*
- **find out** — discover — *I found out the truth from a colleague.*
- **hang around** — loiter — *A few teenagers were hanging around outside the shop.*
- **hang on** — wait; hold — *Hang on a second, I'll be right there.*
- **hang out** — spend time — *We usually hang out at the park after school.*
- **hang up** — end phone call — *She hung up before I could explain.*
- **mix up** — confuse — *I always mix up their names.*
- **pass away** — die — *Her grandfather passed away last spring.*
- **pass by** — go past — *A group of tourists passed by the shop.*
- **pass on** — transmit; die (euphemism) — *Please pass on my regards to your family.*
- **pass out** — faint — *He passed out from the heat.*
- **pick out** — choose — *She picked out a dress for the party.*
- **pick up** — collect; learn — *I'll pick you up from the station at six.*
- **pull off** — succeed in — *Somehow they pulled off a last-minute win.*
- **pull out** — withdraw — *The company pulled out of the deal.*
- **pull over** — stop a vehicle — *The police told him to pull over.*
- **pull through** — recover — *The doctors think she'll pull through.*
- **pull up** — stop (vehicle) — *A taxi pulled up outside the hotel.*
- **run away** — flee — *The dog ran away during the storm.*
- **run into** — meet by chance; collide — *I ran into an old classmate yesterday.*
- **run out** — exhaust supply — *We've run out of milk.*
- **run over** — hit (with vehicle) — *He was nearly run over crossing the street.*
- **see off** — say goodbye to — *We went to the airport to see her off.*
- **see through** — perceive truth — *She saw through his excuse immediately.*
- **set off** — depart; trigger — *We set off before sunrise.*
- **set up** — establish; arrange — *They set up a small business together.*
- **show off** — display proudly — *He loves showing off his new car.*
- **show up** — arrive — *She didn't show up to the meeting.*
- **sort out** — organise; resolve — *Let's sort out this mess before the guests arrive.*
- **stand by** — support; be ready — *I'll stand by whatever decision you make.*
- **stand for** — represent; tolerate — *The letters stand for "as soon as possible".*
- **stand out** — be prominent — *Her work really stood out from the rest.*
- **stand up for** — defend — *He always stands up for his friends.*
- **stay up** — remain awake — *We stayed up late talking.*
- **stick to** — adhere to — *Try to stick to the original plan.*
- **stick up for** — defend — *She always sticks up for her younger brother.*
- **wake up** — stop sleeping — *I woke up at five this morning.*
- **watch out** — be careful — *Watch out, the floor is wet.*
- **wear out** — exhaust; deteriorate — *These shoes have really worn out.*
- **work out** — exercise; solve — *He works out at the gym every morning.*
- **write down** — note — *Write down the address before you forget it.*
