lessons.title: Appendix K. The Connective Words, One by One
lessons.titleRu: Appendix K. Связующие слова, одно за другим
lessons.grammarMd:
Every other part of this book is organised by **topic** — tenses here, relative clauses there. That works when you know what you are looking for. It fails in the one situation learners meet most often: you are halfway through a sentence, you hit a small word that seems to *split* it in two, and you do not know what to call the thing you are looking at, so you cannot look it up.

This appendix is organised by **word**. Its job is to answer the question "what is this word doing here?" for the small set of words that carry English sentence structure — the ones that appear mid-sentence, join or separate the parts, and have almost no meaning of their own.

### K.1 Why these particular words are the hard part

Content words (*dog, run, beautiful*) are learnable one at a time: each has a meaning, a dictionary entry, a translation. The words in this appendix are not like that. Three properties make them different, and all three make them hard to look up:

- **They carry structure, not meaning.** *Of* does not mean anything on its own; it announces that a relationship exists between two nouns and lets the nouns supply what it is. You cannot learn *of* by memorising a translation, because there is nothing to translate.
- **One form does several unrelated jobs.** *That* has four separate grammars (K.3). *As* has five (K.5). Meeting one of them teaches you nothing about the other four, so the word keeps ambushing you.
- **They are invisible until they break something.** A wrong noun is obvious. A wrong connective produces a sentence that is grammatical but says something you did not mean — or a sentence a reader has to re-parse. That is the "sentence that suddenly splits in half" feeling.

The practical consequence: these words repay being learned as a **closed set**, deliberately, the way you would learn irregular verbs — not picked up incidentally.

### K.2 The complete connective inventory

Every word that joins, sorted by the relationship it signals. The **column** matters as much as the word, because the column decides the punctuation and what may follow:

- **Subordinator** — introduces a full clause inside a larger sentence (Chapter 120). Comma when it comes first: *Although it rained, we went.*
- **Coordinator** — joins two equals (Chapter 119). Comma before it when it joins two independent clauses.
- **Linking adverb** — connects across a sentence boundary; it is *not* a conjunction and cannot join two clauses with a comma (Chapter 122, and the comma-splice rule in 167).

| Relationship | Subordinators (+ clause) | Linking adverbs (between sentences) |
|---|---|---|
| **Addition** | — | also, moreover, furthermore, in addition, besides, likewise, what's more |
| **Contrast / concession** | although, though, even though, even if, whereas, while, much as | however, nevertheless, nonetheless, still, yet, on the other hand, instead, conversely |
| **Cause / reason** | because, since, as, for, seeing that, now that, in that | — |
| **Result / effect** | so … that, such … that | therefore, thus, hence, consequently, as a result, accordingly, so |
| **Purpose** | so that, in order that, lest, in case | — |
| **Condition** | if, unless, provided (that), as long as, in case, whether, supposing, given that, on condition that | otherwise, in that case, if so, if not |
| **Time / sequence** | when, while, before, after, until, till, since, as, as soon as, once, whenever, by the time, now that | first, then, next, meanwhile, afterwards, subsequently, finally, earlier |
| **Manner / comparison** | as, as if, as though, than, the way, the … the | similarly, likewise, in the same way |
| **Place** | where, wherever, everywhere | — |
| **Example / restatement** | — | for example, for instance, namely, that is, in particular, in other words |
| **Summary / conclusion** | — | in short, in conclusion, to sum up, overall, all in all |

The **coordinators** are a closed set of exactly seven — *for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so* (FANBOYS, Chapter 119) — and the **correlative pairs** work in two parts: *both … and*, *either … or*, *neither … nor*, *not only … but also*, *whether … or*, *no sooner … than* (Chapter 121). Appendix D lists the linking adverbs by function with example sentences.

### K.3 Reading an unfamiliar connector — a procedure

When a small word stops you mid-sentence, ask these in order:

1. **What follows it — a clause (subject + verb) or just a noun phrase?** A clause means it is a conjunction or a relative word; a bare noun phrase means it is a preposition. This one question separates *because* from *because of*, *although* from *despite*, *while* from *during* (120.6).
2. **Is something missing after it?** If a noun is missing later in the clause, you are in a **relative** clause; if the clause is complete, you have a **complementiser** or an adverbial clause (the gap test, K.3).
3. **Could the sentence stand without this part?** If yes, it is non-defining or parenthetical, and it should have commas (128, 167).
4. **Does the word have another job you already know?** If the reading you assumed produces nonsense, try the other job from K.3–K.7 — this is usually the answer with *that*, *as*, *since*, *for*, and *while*.

### K.4 *And*


The most-used word in English after *the*, and the one learners assume needs no explanation. It does, because *and* is not only addition: the **order of the two halves** can carry meaning that *and* itself never states.

| Job | Example | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| Addition | *bread **and** butter* | pure joining; order is free |
| Sequence | *He came **and** saw the mess.* | "and then" — order is fixed |
| Result / consequence | *Touch it **and** you'll burn.* | "and as a result"; equals a conditional |
| Contrast (weak) | *She's clever **and** she's lazy.* | context supplies the *but* feeling |
| Emphasis by repetition | *We waited **and** waited.* | intensity, not two events |

> *She married and had a child.* / *She had a child and married.*
> Feel the difference: nothing in *and* means "then", yet the two sentences describe different life stories. The sequence is read off the **order of the clauses**, not off the word. This is why reordering coordinated clauses is not a stylistic choice when the events are temporal — it changes the facts.

**The parallelism requirement.** Whatever stands on each side of *and* must be the same kind of thing — two nouns, two verb phrases, two clauses (Chapter 134). ✗ *She likes swimming and to run* breaks it; ✓ *swimming and running* repairs it.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I like tea, and coffee.* → ✓ *I like tea **and** coffee.* **Cause:** no comma before *and* joining two **words**; the comma is only for joining two independent clauses (167).
- ✗ *He is tall and thin and clever and kind.* → ✓ *tall, thin, clever**, and** kind.* **Cause:** in a list, only the last join takes *and*; the rest take commas.
- ✗ *Try and do it* in formal writing → ✓ *Try **to** do it.* **Cause:** *try and* is an idiomatic spoken coordination; formal register wants the infinitive.
- ✗ *She likes swimming and to run.* → ✓ *swimming **and** running.* **Cause:** violated parallelism (134).

### K.5 *As*


One word, five jobs, and the highest ambiguity risk of any connector in English. Chapter 120.2 treats it as a subordinator; this is the whole picture.

| Job | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Reason | ***As** it's late, let's stop.* | weaker than *because*; marks a reason both parties already accept |
| Time / simultaneity | ***As** I left, the phone rang.* | two things at one moment |
| Manner | *Do **as** I say.* | takes a **clause** — contrast *like* + noun (116.1) |
| Comparison | *as white **as** snow* | the *as … as* frame (37.8) |
| Role / capacity | *She works **as** a nurse.* | she **is** one — *like a nurse* = merely resembles one |

> *As she was leaving, he called.*
> Feel the difference: this sentence has two readings and English gives you no way to tell them apart — "while she was leaving" (time) or "because she was leaving" (reason). Both are natural. **When the two readings would lead a listener to different conclusions, abandon *as*** and write *while* or *because*. This is the rare case where the right advice is to avoid a correct word.

**The *as* / *like* boundary is the one that marks you out.** *Like* takes a noun; *as* takes a clause or names a real role. *He works **like** a machine* (tireless, but human). *He works **as** a machine* would mean he *is* one. Informal English increasingly puts *like* before clauses (*like I said*); it is still non-standard in formal writing.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *Do like I say.* → ✓ *Do **as** I say.* **Cause:** a clause follows, so *as* is required in standard register.
- ✗ *She works like a nurse* (meaning that is her job) → ✓ *She works **as** a nurse.* **Cause:** *like* asserts resemblance, not identity — this reverses the meaning rather than weakening it.
- ✗ *As you know that, let's move on.* → ✓ ***As** you know, let's move on.* **Cause:** *as* already subordinates; adding *that* double-marks the clause.
- ✗ *He is as tall than me.* → ✓ *as tall **as** me* / ✓ *taller **than** me.* **Cause:** the equality frame takes *as … as*; *than* belongs only to the comparative (37.8).

### K.6 *Because*


The strongest reason word, and the only one that answers a direct *Why?*. That is its practical definition: if the question *Why?* has just been asked or is implied, *because* is the right word; if the reason is background both speakers already accept, *since* or *as* fits better.

| Form | Takes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ***because*** | a **clause** | *We stopped **because** it rained.* |
| ***because of*** | a **noun phrase** | *We stopped **because of** the rain.* |

That split — clause versus noun phrase — is the single most productive error in this whole appendix, and it recurs with *although/despite*, *while/during*, *if/in case of* (120.6).

> *He resigned because he was ill.* / *He resigned, because he was ill.*
> Feel the difference: without the comma, the reason is the point of the sentence — that is *why* he resigned. With the comma, the resignation is the news and the illness is an afterthought explaining it. The comma converts a tight causal link into a loose parenthetical one, which is why it matters in careful writing (167).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *Because of it rained, we stopped.* → ✓ *Because it rained…* / ✓ *Because of the rain…* **Cause:** *because of* demands a noun phrase; a clause followed, so the *of* has to go.
- ✗ *Because he was late. We started without him.* → ✓ *Because he was late, we started without him.* **Cause:** a *because*-clause is subordinate and cannot stand as a sentence — the classic fragment (216).
- ✗ *The reason is because he was late.* → ✓ *The reason is **that** he was late.* **Cause:** *reason* already means "cause", so *because* repeats it; the slot after *is* needs a noun clause (221 on redundancy).

### K.7 *But*


Taught as "contrast", which covers only its commonest job. *But* has four, and two of them are not contrastive at all.

| Job | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Contrast against expectation | *It's small **but** powerful.* | the core sense: X, yet surprisingly Y |
| Exception ("except") | *Everyone **but** me knew.* | a **preposition** here, not a conjunction |
| The corrective frame | *Not the red one **but** the blue.* | *not X but Y* — replaces, not contrasts |
| *but for* = "if not for" | ***But for** your help, I'd have failed.* | an unreal condition in two words (90.9) |

> *He is poor but honest.* / *He is poor and honest.*
> Feel the difference: *and* simply lists two facts. *But* smuggles in an assumption — that poverty and honesty are somehow in tension, that one would not expect them together. That implication is doing social work the speaker may not intend. Choosing *but* is never neutral; it asserts that the second half is surprising given the first.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *Although it was late, but we continued.* → ✓ *Although it was late, we continued.* **Cause:** double-marking the concession; English allows one connector per join, not one at each end (120.3).
- ✗ *Everyone knew but I.* → ✓ *everyone knew **but me**.* **Cause:** exception-*but* is a preposition, so it takes the object form.
- ✗ *He is not tall but he is short.* → ✓ *He is not tall **but short**.* **Cause:** the *not X but Y* frame joins two like elements; repeating the subject and verb breaks the parallel (134).
- ✗ *But for you helped me…* → ✓ *But for **your help**…* **Cause:** *but for* is a preposition and takes a noun phrase.

### K.8 *For*


*For* is a preposition with five distinct uses and — surprisingly to most learners — also one of the seven coordinating conjunctions. The conjunction is rare and literary; the preposition is everywhere.

| Job | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Duration | *I waited **for** two hours.* | how long — contrast *since* + a point (K.13) |
| Purpose / intended use | *a tool **for** cutting* | takes *-ing*, never a to-infinitive after a noun |
| Beneficiary | *a gift **for** you* | who gets it |
| Exchange / price | *I paid £5 **for** it.* | what was given in return |
| In favour of | *Are you **for** or against?* | the opposite of *against* |
| **Conjunction: "because"** | *He stopped, **for** he was tired.* | literary; always after a comma; cannot start a sentence |

> *I bought a present for my sister.* / *I bought a present to my sister.*
> Feel the difference: the second is simply wrong, and the reason is worth knowing. *To* marks a **destination or recipient of transfer** — *I gave it **to** her* — while *for* marks the **person the act benefits**. *Buy* does not transfer anything to anyone by itself; you buy on someone's behalf. Verbs split into two camps on exactly this, and the camp decides the preposition: *give/send/show/lend* take *to*; *buy/make/cook/find* take *for* (Chapter 136 on ditransitives).

**Duration *for* is the one that disappears.** In *I've lived here for ten years* it is often dropped in speech (*I've lived here ten years*), but never before *since*: ✗ *for since 2010*.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I am here since two hours.* → ✓ *…**for** two hours.* **Cause:** *since* takes a **point** in time, *for* takes a **stretch**. Many languages use one word for both, so this needs deliberate separation (114.4).
- ✗ *a tool for to cut* → ✓ *a tool **for** cutting* / ✓ *a tool **to** cut.* **Cause:** *for* is a preposition and takes *-ing*; the bare purpose-infinitive uses *to* alone. The two structures cannot be merged.
- ✗ *I bought a present to my sister.* → ✓ ***for** my sister.* **Cause:** *buy* is a *for*-verb, not a *to*-verb.
- ✗ *For he was tired, he stopped.* → ✓ *He stopped, **for** he was tired.* / ✓ ***Because** he was tired, he stopped.* **Cause:** conjunction *for* is a coordinator, so it cannot open a sentence or precede its own main clause — unlike the subordinator *because* (119).

### K.9 *How*


The only *wh*-word with no relative use at all: *how* asks questions and heads noun clauses, but never attaches to a noun the way *why*, *where* and *when* can. There is no ✗ *the way how he did it* — the two ways of saying it are *the way he did it* or *how he did it*, never both.

| Job | Example |
|---|---|
| Question of manner | ***How** does it work?* |
| Question of degree (+ adjective/adverb) | ***How** long? **How** often? **How** much?* |
| Noun clause | *Show me **how** it works.* |
| Exclamative | ***How** beautiful!* (165.4) |

> *Show me how it works.* / *Show me how does it work.*
> Feel the difference: the second is the single most common error with embedded *wh*-words. Once a *wh*-word is **inside** a sentence rather than starting a question, the clause reverts to **statement order** — subject before verb, no auxiliary inversion. The question form survives only in a direct question.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I don't know how does it work.* → ✓ *…**how it works**.* **Cause:** embedded clauses take statement order (159).
- ✗ *the way how he did it* → ✓ *the way he did it* / ✓ *how he did it.* **Cause:** *how* and *the way* are alternatives, not partners; using both double-marks the manner.
- ✗ *How is the weather like?* → ✓ *What is the weather **like**?* / ✓ ***How** is the weather?* **Cause:** *like* already asks for a description, so it pairs with *what*; *how* asks directly and needs no *like*.

### K.10 *If*


*If* does **two completely different jobs**, and both look identical from outside — which is why it is the word most likely to split a sentence in a way you did not intend.

| Job | Example | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Condition** | *I'll come **if** you ask.* | adverbial clause — the circumstance under which the main clause holds (84–90) |
| **Embedded yes/no question** | *I don't know **if** it works.* | noun clause — the object of *know*; reported form of *Does it work?* (95) |

**The test:** try replacing *if* with **whether**. Survives → embedded question. Collapses → condition.

- *I don't know **whether** it works.* ✓ → embedded question.
- ✗ *I'll come **whether** you ask.* (the meaning changes entirely) → so the original was a condition.

> *Tell me if you need help.*
> Feel the difference — this sentence genuinely has both readings. As a **condition**: "in the event that you need help, tell me" — say nothing unless the need arises. As an **embedded question**: "tell me whether or not you need help" — answer me now, either way. Native speakers disambiguate by context and intonation; in writing, if the difference matters, rewrite: *Tell me **whether** you need help* forces the second, ***If** you need help, tell me* forces the first.

**Where *whether* is compulsory and *if* is impossible** (95.3): before *or* (*whether it works **or** not*); before a to-infinitive (*I don't know **whether** to go*, never ✗ *if to go*); directly after a preposition (*the question **of whether** it works*); and when the clause is the **subject** (***Whether** he comes is up to him*).

**Two more jobs:** ***if only*** for a wish or regret, taking the backshifted forms of *wish* (*If only I **had** more time* — Chapter 91); and the fixed politeness frame *I was wondering **if** you could…* (307).

**No future after *if***, exactly as with *when*: ✓ *If it **rains**, we'll stay.* ✗ *If it will rain.* The one exception is *will* meaning willingness rather than futurity: *If you'**ll** wait here, I'll fetch him.*

**Common errors**

- ✗ *If it will rain, we'll stay.* → ✓ *If it **rains**…* **Cause:** the condition clause carries no future marker; the main clause carries it for both (63).
- ✗ *I don't know if to go.* → ✓ *…**whether** to go.* **Cause:** only *whether* survives before a to-infinitive.
- ✗ *If I would have known…* → ✓ *If I **had** known…* **Cause:** the third conditional puts the past perfect in the *if*-clause and *would have* only in the main clause (88).
- ✗ *I'll ask him if he will come or not.* → ✓ *…**whether** he will come or not.* **Cause:** before *or not*, *whether* is required.

### K.11 *Of* — the great linker of nouns


*Of* is the most frequent preposition in English and the one this book's preposition chapters (112–117) deliberately leave out, because it fits none of their categories: it is not spatial, not temporal, not directional. Trying to learn it as "a preposition meaning X" fails, because there is no X. **It is a pure grammatical connector between two nouns**, and the relationship it signals is supplied entirely by the nouns on either side of it.

That is why it feels like it splits sentences. It is doing structural work, silently, the way a case ending would in another language — and in fact that is exactly what it replaced.

**The one hard rule: *of* cannot join clauses.** It is never a conjunction. Whatever follows it is a noun phrase; there is never a subject-plus-verb after it. Any sentence where you feel a clause coming after *of* needs a different word — usually *that* (K.3) or a *wh*-word:

- ✗ *the fact **of** he lied* → ✓ *the fact **that** he lied*
- ✗ *the question **of** it works* → ✓ *the question **of whether** it works* (*whether* nominalises the clause first; only then can *of* take it — K.6)

**The relations *of* can carry**

| Relation | Example | The test |
|---|---|---|
| Belonging (of a thing) | *the leg **of** the table* | could be *'s* if the owner were a person |
| Partition / quantity | *some **of** them · a piece **of** cake · most **of** it* | X is a part taken from Y (294) |
| Material / composition | *made **of** wood · a wall **of** stone* | Y is what X is made from |
| Content / measure | *a cup **of** tea · a kilo **of** rice* | X is the container, Y the contents |
| Apposition ("which is") | *the city **of** Rome · the art **of** cooking* | X **is** Y — the two name one thing |
| Subject of an action | *the arrival **of** the train* | = *the train arrived* (192, nominalisation) |
| Object of an action | *the destruction **of** the city* | = *someone destroyed the city* |
| After fixed adjectives and verbs | *afraid **of** · proud **of** · consist **of** · think **of*** | not choosable — learn with the word (117.2) |

The last three rows are where *of* stops being decorative and becomes genuinely ambiguous. *The shooting of the hunters* can mean the hunters shot, or the hunters were shot — English does not distinguish them, and only context does (192.4).

> *a picture **of** my brother* / *a picture **by** my brother* / *my brother's picture*
> Feel the difference: the first shows him — he is the content. The second was painted by him — he is the agent. The third is ambiguous between the two and adds a third reading, that he simply owns it. This is why *of* is not a translation of the genitive but only overlaps with it: English has three constructions where many languages have one case.

**The *'s* / *of* boundary.** As a first approximation, *'s* for people and animals, *of* for things: *the girl's name*, but *the name **of** the street*. The real rule is a scale of animacy and topicality, and both are possible in the middle of it (*the company's decision* / *the decision of the company*), with *'s* favoured when the possessor is the topic being discussed. Chapter 21.4 sets out the full boundary; the practical version is that *'s* on an inanimate object sounds wrong unless the phrase is fixed (*a day's work*, *the water's edge*).

**The double genitive is correct English.** *A friend **of** mine*, *that car **of** his*, *a painting **of** Turner's* — the apparent doubling of possession is standard and has been for centuries. It is not redundancy; it does real work: *a picture of Turner* (he is in it) versus *a picture of Turner's* (he painted or owned it). Chapter 263 covers it in full.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *He is afraid from dogs.* → ✓ *afraid **of** dogs.* **Cause:** the preposition after an adjective is fixed by the adjective, not by logic, and it differs across languages — Russian «бояться» takes the genitive with no preposition at all, so there is no native cue to copy (117.2).
- ✗ *the fact of he lied* → ✓ *the fact **that** he lied.* **Cause:** *of* takes a noun phrase; a clause needs a complementiser.
- ✗ *I could of gone.* → ✓ *I could **have** gone.* **Cause:** in speech *have* reduces to /əv/, identical to *of*; the error is purely orthographic and never occurs in speech (Chapter 10 on connected speech, 217 on confusables).
- ✗ *a table's leg* → ✓ *the leg **of** the table.* **Cause:** an inanimate possessor resists *'s* outside fixed expressions.
- ✗ *most of people* → ✓ *most **of the** people* / ✓ *most people.* **Cause:** partitive *of* requires a **definite** second element — *of* + *the/my/these* — while a bare generic noun takes no *of* at all (205.2).
- ✗ *He consists of three parts the team.* → ✓ *The team **consists of** three parts.* **Cause:** *consist of* is a fixed verb + preposition unit; the *of*-phrase cannot be separated from it (117.1).

### K.12 *Since*


Two meanings in one word, and they are not related: **time** and **reason**. Which one is meant is decided by the tense of the main clause and by position, not by *since* itself.

| Job | Example | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| Time — from a point up to now | *I've known her **since** 2010.* | pulls a **perfect** tense; takes a point, not a stretch |
| Reason — a cause already known | ***Since** you're here, help me.* | usually first in the sentence; no perfect needed |

> *Since he arrived, everything has changed.* / *Since he arrived, we could finally start.*
> Feel the difference: identical opening, two different words. The first is **time** — the present perfect in the main clause forces it: change has been accumulating from that moment to now. The second is **reason** — no perfect, and the logic is causal. The main clause tells you which *since* you are reading, which is why the tense is not decoration.

**Time *since* takes a point, *for* takes a stretch** — the single most reliable pairing in the tense system: *since Monday*, *since I was ten*, *since the war*; but *for three days*, *for ages*, *for a long time* (114.4).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I am here since Monday.* → ✓ *I have **been** here since Monday.* **Cause:** time-*since* requires a perfect; the present simple cannot express a stretch reaching the present (53).
- ✗ *since three years* → ✓ *for three years* / ✓ *since three years **ago***. **Cause:** *since* needs a point; *three years* is a duration, and only *ago* converts it into a point.
- ✗ *Since it was raining, so we stayed.* → ✓ *Since it was raining, we stayed.* **Cause:** double-marking — *since* already subordinates, so *so* is redundant.

### K.13 *So*


Three unrelated structures share this word, and mixing them is one of the most common intermediate errors.

| Job | Structure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Result (coordinator) | *…, **so** + clause* | *It was late, **so** we left.* |
| Purpose (subordinator) | ***so that** + clause with a modal* | *I left early **so that** I could catch it.* |
| Degree | ***so** + adjective/adverb + **that*** | *It was **so** cold **that** we left.* |
| Substitute for a clause | *I think **so**. I hope **so**.* | replaces a whole clause (197) |
| Agreement | ***So** do I.* | with inversion (160.2) |

> *I left early so I could catch the train.* / *I left early, so I could catch the train.*
> Feel the difference: the comma changes the meaning. Without it, *so* = *so that* — purpose: catching the train was the **aim** of leaving early. With it, *so* = result: leaving early **had the effect** that catching it became possible. One comma flips intention into consequence.

**The *so* / *such* split** is decided by what follows: *so* + adjective or adverb alone (*so cold*, *so quickly*); *such* + a noun phrase (*such a mess*, *such good news*). ✗ *so a big mistake* → ✓ *such a big mistake* or ✓ *so big a mistake* (207).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *It was so cold, that we left.* → ✓ *It was so cold **that** we left.* **Cause:** the *so … that* frame is one unit; a comma inside it separates what belongs together.
- ✗ *I was so tired that I couldn't to sleep.* → ✓ *…couldn't **sleep**.* **Cause:** the error is in the modal, not in *so*; modals take a bare infinitive.
- ✗ *such tired* → ✓ *so tired.* **Cause:** *tired* is an adjective standing alone, so it takes *so*.
- ✗ *I think it.* → ✓ *I think **so**.* **Cause:** *so* is the pro-form that stands for a whole clause; *it* stands only for a noun (197.2).

### K.14 *That* — one spelling, four grammars


*That* is the most overloaded structural word in English, and the reason is historical rather than perverse: three originally distinct words converged on one spelling as Old English lost its inflections (Chapter 303.5). Modern English therefore uses a single form for four jobs that most languages keep apart — and Russian keeps apart to this day, with «что», «который», «тот» and «такой … что» all being different words. Learning to see which of the four you are looking at removes a surprising amount of what feels like "hard grammar," because most hard-looking English sentences contain at least one *that*.

**The four jobs**

| # | Job | Example | Can it be dropped? | Russian equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Complementiser** — a bare marker introducing a noun clause | *I know **(that)** it works.* | usually yes (127.3) | что |
| 2 | **Relative pronoun** — introduces a relative clause, leaving a gap | *the book **that** I read __* | yes, if it is the object (128) | который |
| 3 | **Demonstrative** — the only one carrying real meaning ("the distant one") | ***that** book* · *I want **that**.* | no — it means something | тот |
| 4 | **Degree / result frame** | *so cold **that** I left* · *such a mess **that** we gave up* | no | такой … что |

**The gap test — how to tell 1 from 2, which is the only pair that genuinely confuses people.** A relative clause is *missing a noun*; a complementiser clause is *complete*.

> *the fact **that** he lied* / *the lie **that** he told __*
> Feel the difference: read each clause on its own. *He lied* is a whole sentence — nothing is missing, so *that* is a bare marker introducing it, and it is job 1. *He told __* is not a whole sentence — *told* has lost its object, and the missing object **is** *the lie*, so *that* is standing in for a noun, and it is job 2. The test is mechanical and it never fails: **look for the hole.**

That single test also predicts droppability, which is why it is worth doing rather than guessing. Job 1 drops freely (*I know it works*). Job 2 drops only when the missing noun is the **object** (*the book I read*), never when it is the **subject**: ✗ *the man fixed my car* has lost the join entirely, because *that* was holding the subject slot (128).

**Why the demonstrative is the easy one.** Job 3 is the only *that* with lexical meaning, so it is the only one you can stress: *I want **THAT**, not this.* Try stressing the others and the sentence breaks — ✗ *I know **THAT** it works* forces a demonstrative reading and turns *that* into the object of *know*. Stress is therefore a second, independent check.

**Related frames worth recognising as single units**, because parsing them word by word wastes effort: *the fact that…* (appositive — job 1 attached to a noun), *so that…* (purpose, K.9), *now that…* (reason plus time), *in that…* (formal "because"), *not that…* (dismissing an alternative: *Not that it matters*).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *The book that I read it was good.* → ✓ *The book **that** I read was good.* **Cause:** the relative *that* already fills the object slot; adding *it* fills it twice. This is the single commonest relative-clause error among speakers of languages that use a resumptive pronoun, and Russian is one of them — «книга, которую я её прочитал» is equally wrong in Russian, which makes this an error of carelessness rather than interference.
- ✗ *I know that he. He is late.* → ✓ *I know **that** he is late.* **Cause:** job 1 must introduce a **whole clause**; it cannot introduce a bare noun.
- ✗ *the man that fixed my car* → this is in fact ✓ correct; *that* may introduce a subject relative on a person, and the older prescription that *who* is obligatory for people has no support in usage (128.7). **Cause of the confusion:** *that* is barred from **non-defining** clauses, not from people — ✗ *My brother, that lives in Rome, …* → ✓ *My brother, **who** lives in Rome, …*
- ✗ *He said me that he was tired.* → ✓ *He **told** me that…* / ✓ *He said that…* **Cause:** the error is not in *that* but in the verb pattern; *say* takes no indirect object without *to* (218.11).
- ✗ *It was so a big mistake that…* → ✓ *It was **such a** big mistake that…* / ✓ *so big a mistake* **Cause:** job 4 splits by what follows — *so* + adjective, *such* + noun phrase (207).

### K.15 *To*


Two unrelated jobs sharing one spelling, and the boundary between them causes a specific, very common error.

| Job | What follows | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Preposition** | a **noun phrase** | *I gave it **to** him.* · *I went **to** London.* |
| **Infinitive marker** | a **bare verb** | *I want **to** go.* · *easy **to** understand.* |

> *I look forward to see you.* / *I look forward to seeing you.*
> Feel the difference — only the second is English, and the reason is that in *look forward to*, the *to* is the **preposition**, not the infinitive marker. Prepositions take nouns, and the noun form of a verb is the *-ing* form. The test: **can you replace *to* with *towards*?** *Look forward towards…* is close enough to work, so it is the preposition → use *-ing*. In *I want to go*, ✗ *want towards* is nonsense → infinitive marker → bare verb.

The expressions where *to* is the preposition are a closed list worth memorising: *look forward to*, *be/get used to*, *object to*, *be committed to*, *in addition to*, *when it comes to*, *be opposed to*, *confess to* (183, 117.1).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I'm used to get up early.* → ✓ *…used to **getting** up early.* **Cause:** *be used to* (= accustomed) has prepositional *to*. Contrast *used to get up early* (a past habit), where *used to* is a different construction entirely with a bare infinitive — the two look almost identical and mean different things (183).
- ✗ *I want that you come.* → ✓ *I want **you to come**.* **Cause:** *want* takes an object plus a to-infinitive, never a *that*-clause — one of the sharpest differences from most European languages (99.4a).
- ✗ *He is interested to learn Spanish.* → ✓ *interested **in learning**.* **Cause:** the preposition is fixed by the adjective; *interested* selects *in* (117.2).
- ✗ *I go to home.* → ✓ *I go **home**.* **Cause:** *home*, *here*, *there*, *abroad*, *upstairs* are adverbs of place and take no preposition (117.6).

### K.16 *What*


*What* is the *wh*-word that most often surprises learners, because one of its three jobs has no equivalent in many languages: it can introduce a clause that **is itself the subject or object** of the sentence, with no noun anywhere for it to attach to.

| Job | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Question word | ***What** happened?* | asks for open information |
| Noun clause (embedded question) | *I know **what** you mean.* | statement order inside |
| **Free relative** | ***What I need** is time.* | = *the thing that I need* — no antecedent |
| *What* + noun | ***What** time is it?* · ***What** a mess!* | determiner, and exclamative (153.1, 165.4) |

> *What I need is time.* / *That I need time is obvious.*
> Feel the difference: both start with a clause acting as subject, but *what* **contains its own antecedent** — it packages "the thing which" into one word — while *that* merely introduces a statement. This is why *what* can never be replaced by *that* in the first sentence: ✗ *That I need is time.* The free relative is also the machinery behind the *wh*-cleft, the standard way English foregrounds something (169).

***What* is not a relative pronoun on a noun.** After a noun, English needs *that* or *which*: ✗ *the book what I read* → ✓ *the book **that** I read*. The *what*-form exists in some dialects but is non-standard.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *the film what I saw* → ✓ *the film **that** I saw.* **Cause:** *what* carries its own antecedent, so it cannot follow one — the noun is already there.
- ✗ *I don't know what is your name.* → ✓ *…**what your name is**.* **Cause:** embedded clauses take statement order (159).
- ✗ *What is your opinion about?* (meaning "what do you think of it") → ✓ *What do you think **of** it?* **Cause:** a stranded preposition must have something to strand from; here the object was never established.
- ✗ *What a beautiful is this place!* → ✓ ***What** a beautiful place this is!* **Cause:** the *what*-exclamative takes *what* + (a/an) + adjective + **noun**, then the subject and verb (165.4).

### K.17 *When*


Three jobs, and one rule that catches nearly every learner regardless of first language.

| Job | Example |
|---|---|
| Time subordinator | *Call me **when** you arrive.* |
| Embedded question | *I don't know **when** he left.* |
| Relative adverb (on a time noun) | *the day **when** we met* |

**The rule: no future tense inside a *when*-clause.** ✓ *I'll call **when** I arrive.* ✗ *when I will arrive.* The main clause carries the future for both halves. The same applies after *if*, *until*, *before*, *after*, *as soon as*, *once* — the whole family (63).

> *When he arrives, we'll start.* / *I don't know when he'll arrive.*
> Feel the difference — and note that the second **does** take *will*, which looks like a contradiction. It is not: the ban applies only to the **time-subordinator** *when*. In the second sentence *when* heads an **embedded question**, which is a noun clause, and noun clauses take whatever tense the meaning requires. So the test is not the word but the job: is this clause telling you *when something happens* (no future) or *asking which time it is* (future allowed)?

**Common errors**

- ✗ *When I will finish, I'll call you.* → ✓ *When I **finish**…* **Cause:** time clause, so no future marker (63).
- ✗ *I remember when was I young.* → ✓ *…**when I was** young.* **Cause:** embedded clauses take statement order (159).
- ✗ *the time when that we met* → ✓ *the time **when** we met* / ✓ *the time **that** we met.* **Cause:** *when* and *that* are alternatives here, not partners.

### K.18 *Where*


| Job | Example |
|---|---|
| Place subordinator | *Put it **where** I can see it.* |
| Embedded question | *Tell me **where** it is.* |
| Relative adverb (on a place noun) | *the house **where** I grew up* |

The relative use has a formal alternative that shows what *where* is really doing: *the house **in which** I grew up*. *Where* = preposition + *which*, packed into one word. That equivalence explains why ✗ *the house where I grew up in* is wrong — the *in* is already inside *where*, so writing it again strands a duplicate (128).

> *This is the place where he died.* / *This is the place that he died in.*
> Feel the difference: none in meaning — both are correct, and the choice is register. *Where* is the neutral everyday form; *in which* is formal; *that … in* is the most colloquial. What you cannot do is combine the first with the third.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *the house where I live in* → ✓ *the house **where** I live* / ✓ *the house **that** I live **in**.* **Cause:** *where* already contains the preposition.
- ✗ *I know where is the station.* → ✓ *…**where the station is**.* **Cause:** embedded statement order (159).
- ✗ *the situation where you must decide* → acceptable in speech, but ✓ *the situation **in which** you must decide* is preferred in formal writing. **Cause:** *where* strictly marks physical place; extending it to abstract nouns is common but informal.

### K.19 *Whether*


The formal twin of *if*, and the one that survives in four positions where *if* cannot appear at all (95.3).

| Position | *whether* | *if* |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary embedded question | *I don't know **whether** it works.* | ✓ also *if* |
| Before *or (not)* | *…**whether** it works **or not**.* | ✗ |
| Before a to-infinitive | *I don't know **whether** to go.* | ✗ |
| After a preposition | *the question **of whether** it works* | ✗ |
| As the subject | ***Whether** he comes is up to him.* | ✗ |

> *Let me know if you're coming.* / *Let me know whether you're coming.*
> Feel the difference: the first is ambiguous — it can mean "only contact me in the event that you come." The second cannot: it asks for an answer either way. In writing, where intonation cannot disambiguate, *whether* is the precise choice, and this is the main practical reason to prefer it.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I doubt if to accept.* → ✓ *…**whether** to accept.* **Cause:** only *whether* precedes a to-infinitive.
- ✗ *It depends of whether he comes.* → ✓ *depends **on** whether…* **Cause:** the error is the preposition selected by *depend*, not *whether* (117.1).
- ✗ *Whether or not if he comes…* → ✓ ***Whether or not** he comes…* **Cause:** *whether* and *if* are alternatives; using both double-marks the clause.

### K.20 *Which*


| Job | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Question word (closed choice) | ***Which** one do you want?* | from a known set — contrast *what*, open (28.4) |
| Embedded question | *Ask **which** he prefers.* | statement order |
| Relative on a thing | *the book, **which** I loved,* | non-defining, with commas |
| Relative on a **whole clause** | *He was late, **which** annoyed me.* | refers to the entire preceding clause (128.9) |

> *Which book do you want?* / *What book do you want?*
> Feel the difference: *which* implies a **known, limited set** — the books on this table. *What* leaves the set open — any book at all. Choosing *which* silently tells your listener that the options are already established, which is why *Which country are you from?* sounds odd unless a list has been named.

**The whole-clause relative is the one worth mastering**, because it has no equivalent in many languages and is very common in writing: *She missed the train, **which** meant she was late.* Here *which* does not refer to the train — it refers to the whole fact of missing it. It always takes a comma, and *that* can never replace it.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *the book which I read it* → ✓ *the book **which** I read.* **Cause:** the relative already fills the object slot (K.3).
- ✗ *He was late which annoyed me.* → ✓ *He was late**,** which annoyed me.* **Cause:** the whole-clause relative is always non-defining and takes a comma.
- ✗ *My car, that is red, is outside.* → ✓ *My car, **which** is red, is outside.* **Cause:** *that* is barred from non-defining clauses (128.7).

### K.21 *While*


| Job | Example |
|---|---|
| Simultaneity | *I cooked **while** she read.* |
| Contrast | ***While** I agree with the aim, I doubt the method.* |

The contrast use is a softer *although*: it concedes rather than opposes. Position disambiguates in practice — clause-initial *while* is usually contrast, mid-sentence *while* is usually time.

> *While she was working, he cooked.* / *While she works hard, he does nothing.*
> Feel the difference: identical shape, different jobs. The first is two things happening at once. The second sets one fact against another and implies a judgement. The tense is the clue — a progressive after *while* points to time; a simple present pointing at a general truth points to contrast (120.5).

***While* takes a clause; *during* takes a noun.** ✗ *during I was there* → ✓ *while I was there* / ✓ *during my stay* (120.6).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *During I was reading, he called.* → ✓ ***While** I was reading…* **Cause:** *during* is a preposition and needs a noun phrase.
- ✗ *While to work, I listen to music.* → ✓ *While **working**…* / ✓ *While **I work**…* **Cause:** *while* takes a clause or a participle, never a to-infinitive.

### K.22 *Who / whom / whose*


| Word | Role | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **who** | subject | *the man **who** called* |
| **whom** | object, and after a preposition | *the man **whom** I met* · *to **whom** it may concern* |
| **whose** | possessive — for people **and things** | *the man **whose** car…* · *a house **whose** roof leaks* |

**The *who/whom* test:** replace with *he/him*. If *he* fits, use *who*; if *him* fits, use *whom* (the *m* is the memory hook). *I met him* → *the man **whom** I met*. In modern English *whom* survives reliably only directly after a preposition (*to whom*, *for whom*); elsewhere *who* is normal and *whom* can sound stiff (28.2).

> *the man who I met* / *the man whom I met* / *the man I met*
> Feel the difference: all three are used, and they differ only in register. The third — dropping the pronoun entirely — is the commonest in speech and is fully correct whenever the relative is the **object**. It is impossible when the relative is the subject: ✗ *the man called me yesterday* (meaning "the man who called me") loses the join.

***Whose* is not restricted to people**, despite its resemblance to *who*: *a book whose cover is torn* is standard, and the alternative *the cover of which* is formal and heavy (28.3).

**Common errors**

- ✗ *Who did you give it to?* in formal writing → ✓ *To **whom** did you give it?* **Cause:** after a fronted preposition, *whom* is required; the *who…to* version is correct in speech (117.4).
- ✗ *the man which I met* → ✓ *the man **who/whom/that** I met.* **Cause:** *which* is for things.
- ✗ *the man who's car…* → ✓ *the man **whose** car…* **Cause:** *who's* = *who is*; the possessive has no apostrophe, exactly as with *its* (171).

### K.23 *Why*


Mid-sentence, *why* is never asking a question. It is doing one of two things, and both are easy to spot once you know to look.

| Job | Example | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Head of a noun clause | *I don't know **why** he left.* | the whole clause is the object of *know*; delete it and the sentence is incomplete |
| Relative adverb | *the reason **why** he left* | attaches to a noun of reason; usually droppable |

> *I don't know why he left.* / *I don't know why did he leave.*
> Feel the difference — the second is simply wrong, and it is the commonest *wh*-error there is. Once *why* is **inside** a sentence, the clause takes **statement order**: subject, then verb, no inversion, no auxiliary *do*. The question form belongs only to a direct question: *Why did he leave?*

**The relative *why* is nearly always optional.** *The reason **why** he left* = *the reason he left* = *the reason **that** he left*. All three are correct; the bare version is commonest. What you cannot do is use *why* after a noun that is not about reason: ✗ *the day why we met* → ✓ *the day **when** we met*.

***Why* also has two small idiomatic uses** worth recognising: ***Why not?*** as an agreement or a suggestion (*Why not ask her?*), and the archaic-sounding discourse marker *Why, of course!*, which survives mostly in older writing and set phrases.

**Common errors**

- ✗ *I don't know why did he leave.* → ✓ *…**why he left**.* **Cause:** embedded statement order (159).
- ✗ *I don't know, why he left.* → ✓ *I don't know **why** he left.* **Cause:** no comma before an embedded *wh*-clause in English, unlike many languages (167).
- ✗ *the day why we met* → ✓ *the day **when** we met.* **Cause:** each relative adverb selects its own kind of noun — *why* for reason, *when* for time, *where* for place.
- ✗ *That's the reason why because he left.* → ✓ *That's **why** he left.* / ✓ *That's the reason he left.* **Cause:** three ways of marking the same reason, stacked; pick one (221).

### K.24 The remaining connectives, briefly

Everything else in the inventory of K.2 that earns a note of its own:

- ***because*** — the strongest reason word, and the only one that answers a direct *Why?*. Compare *since* and *as*, which mark a reason already known to both parties, and *for*, which is literary (120.4, K.6). ***Because of*** takes a **noun**, not a clause: *because of the rain*, but *because it rained* (120.6).
- ***to*** — two unrelated jobs. **Preposition**: *I gave it **to** him*, *I went **to** London* — a noun follows. **Infinitive marker**: *I want **to** go* — a bare verb follows (285.1). The trap is the handful of expressions where *to* is the *preposition* and therefore takes *-ing*: *look forward **to** seeing you*, *be used **to** living here*, *object **to** paying* (183, 117.1). Ask whether *to* could be replaced by *towards*; if yes, it is the preposition, so use *-ing*.
- ***than*** — comparison only, and it takes the **object** form of a pronoun in ordinary use (*taller **than** me*), the subject form when a verb follows (*taller **than** I am*) — 37.5.
- ***unless*** — "except if", a negative condition. It is not always interchangeable with *if not*: *unless* states the single circumstance that would cancel the main clause, so it resists non-cancelling contexts — ✓ *I'll be upset **if** you don't come*, ✗ *I'll be upset **unless** you come* is odd because your coming is not what prevents the upset (90.1).
- ***although / though / even though / whereas*** — concession. *Though* can also end a sentence as an adverb (*It's late. I'll come, **though**.*); *even though* is the emphatic version; *whereas* is for direct contrast between two facts, not for concession (120.3).
- ***until / till*** — "up to the moment when", and like *when* it takes no future inside: *Wait **until** I **come** back.* *Till* is the same word informally; *by* is different — a deadline, not a stretch (114.3).
- ***once / as soon as / whenever*** — time subordinators with the same no-future rule. *Once* = "as soon as, and from then on"; *whenever* = "every time that" or "no matter when".
- ***nor / yet*** — the two FANBOYS people forget. *Nor* joins two negatives and **inverts** what follows (*He didn't call, **nor** did he write*); *yet* is a coordinator meaning "but nevertheless" (*small **yet** powerful*).
- ***either / neither / both*** — correlatives that must be **balanced**: *either X **or** Y*, *neither X **nor** Y*, *both X **and** Y*, with the same kind of thing on each side (Chapter 121, 134).
- ***like* vs *as*** — *like* takes a **noun** (*He works **like** a machine* — resembling one); *as* takes a **clause** or names a real role (*Do **as** I say*; *She works **as** a nurse* — she is one). Informal English increasingly uses *like* before a clause; it is still marked as non-standard in formal writing (116.1).
- ***so that / in order that / lest*** — purpose, taking a clause with a modal (*so that he **could** hear*). Distinct from result *so … that* and from plain coordinator *so* (K.7, 207).
- ***as if / as though*** — hypothetical manner, often with the unreal past: *He talks **as if** he **knew** everything.*

Every word below has its own deep entry above. This table is the way in: find the word, jump to its section.

The previous thirty-one parts gave you the rules, one construction at a time: the parts of speech, the tenses, the voices, the moods, the clause types, the order words fall into. Knowing a rule and being able to *find* it in a real sentence are two different skills, and beginners routinely assume that understanding a rule means they can automatically spot it at work. They can't — not yet. Recognising a gerund sitting on its own (*Swimming is fun.*) is easy. Finding the one gerund buried inside a twenty-word sentence that also contains a participle, an infinitive, and a noun clause is a different order of task, and it is the one that actually matters every time you read a paragraph, listen to a fast speaker, or try to build a long sentence of your own without losing track of what agrees with what. This part builds that second skill. It teaches you to look at any English sentence — however long, however tangled — and identify every word's part of speech, every phrase's internal structure, and every clause's job, one layer at a time. This is, without exaggeration, the single best exercise for turning grammar you *know* into grammar you *use without thinking*. Chapter 237 is the core of it: fifteen worked sentences, each adding exactly one new complication to the last, so that by the end you are confidently parsing constructions — cleft sentences, dangling-participle traps, three-deep stacks of modifiers — that would have looked impenetrable at the start. The chapters that follow this one build on the same method with diagrams, harder tiers, and a final checklist; this chapter gives you the method itself, worked all the way through, in full sentences, with every choice explained rather than asserted.
